The core operator is the empirical win rate estimator, defined as r = W/(W+L), which is subject to sampling variance. In the full dataset, r = 0.527 with a 95% confidence interval [0.5008, 0.5786]. This interval includes the break-even probability of 0.52381, suggesting no statistically significant edge. The z-score of 0.797 fails to exceed 1.96, confirming insignificance. The negative ROI of -5.48% arises because even though the model wins more than half the time, payouts are structured such that the house edge dominates. The confidence intervals decrease in precision with increasing confidence levels, showing that higher confidence bands do not improve performance—this is a form of regression toward the mean. The model's calibration layer, fitted on live data, is tested out-of-sample against 27 seasons of historical data, yielding consistent negative returns. The lack of evidence for superior performance in any subset indicates that the model lacks predictive power beyond random chance. The failure mode lies in assuming that high-confidence predictions translate into profitable outcomes without considering the structural bias in betting payouts.
